orgs.title: Job Application for Senior Backend Engineer, Fleet Platform at Northwind Robotics

answers.question: Why do you want to work at Northwind Robotics?
answers.answer: I've wanted to work on software that moves physical things for a long time, and Northwind Robotics is one of the few companies where the backend really is the product. When I read your engineering post about how Northwind Dispatch reassigns picks when a robot's battery drops mid-route, I recognized the exact problem I spent four years on in freight routing, except your version has to answer in milliseconds instead of minutes. I like that Northwind Dispatch runs inside customer warehouses rather than in a demo lab, because it means the hard parts are the unglamorous ones: flaky networks, partial failures, and operators who need to override the system at 2am. That's the work I'm best at and the work I want more of. I also appreciated that the interview process includes debugging a real past incident. It told me the team cares about how systems fail, not only how they look on a whiteboard.
answers.form: Job Application for Senior Backend Engineer, Fleet Platform at Northwind Robotics

answers.question: What has been your proudest professional accomplishment?
answers.answer: The project I'm proudest of is a billing migration I led two years ago. Our invoices were generated by a nightly batch job that had grown to eleven hours, and when it failed, which happened about twice a month, finance had to reconcile by hand for days. I proposed moving to event-driven invoicing, where each usage event updates a running ledger and the invoice is just a snapshot of it. The hard part wasn't the code. It was proving the new system produced the same numbers as the old one. I built a shadow mode that ran both pipelines side by side for six weeks and diffed every invoice line, and we found forty-one discrepancies, most of them bugs in the old job that customers had been quietly overpaying or underpaying for years. We cut over one customer segment at a time, with a one-click rollback that we never had to use. Month-end close went from four days to under one, and the on-call rotation stopped dreading the first of the month. I'm proud of it because the result was invisible to customers, which is exactly what a billing migration should be, and because two engineers who joined mid-project now own the system and have extended it without me.
answers.form: Job Application for Senior Backend Engineer, Fleet Platform at Northwind Robotics

answers.question: How do you work with cross-functional partners such as product managers and designers?
answers.answer: I try to get involved before there's a spec. When a product manager is still deciding what to build, a short conversation about what's cheap and what's expensive saves weeks later, so I ask to sit in on early customer calls and I write up technical constraints in plain language. With designers, I share rough prototypes early, even ugly ones, because it's easier to argue about something on screen than about a mockup that can't show loading states or errors. I also try to be explicit about trade-offs instead of just saying no. If a request would take six weeks, I'll say what we could ship in two and what we'd give up. When we disagree, I'd rather write the options down side by side with their costs and let the person who owns the decision make it. On my last team I started a fifteen-minute weekly sync between engineering, design and support, and it cut the number of surprise bug reports after launches roughly in half.
answers.form: Job Application for Senior Backend Engineer, Fleet Platform at Northwind Robotics

answers.question: Additional Information
answers.answer: A few things that didn't fit elsewhere on the form. My notice period is four weeks, and I can start sooner if the timing matters for the team. I took six months off between roles to care for a family member; I kept my skills current during that time by contributing fixes to an open-source job queue library, and I'm happy to talk about that period in an interview. I'm comfortable working remotely or in a hybrid setup, and I've worked across time zones for most of my career. If it helps, I can share a design review and a postmortem I wrote, with identifying details removed, as work samples.

answers.question: Why Larkspur Health?
answers.answer: My mom is a home health nurse, and for years I've watched her finish her visits and then spend another hour at the kitchen table catching up on charting. When I tried Larkspur Chart during a friend's demo, the first thing I noticed was that it saved notes offline and synced when the connection came back, which is exactly what she complains about in patients' homes with no signal. That told me Larkspur Health is building for the people doing the work, not for the billing department. I'm also drawn to the reliability bar. Software that clinicians depend on can't have a bad deploy on a Friday afternoon, and I want to work somewhere that treats on-call, data integrity and careful rollouts as part of the product rather than as overhead. I've spent most of my career on systems where a wrong number costs money. At Larkspur Health a wrong number could cost something more important, and I want my work to matter in that way.

answers.question: Tell us about a time you failed. What did you learn?
answers.answer: At Halcyon Freight I owned the upgrade of our shipment tracking database to a newer Postgres version. I tested the upgrade on a staging copy, it went fine, and I scheduled the production cutover for a Saturday morning. What I hadn't accounted for was size: one table in production was forty times larger than in staging, and an index rebuild that took four minutes in staging took more than three hours in production. Customer tracking pages were read-only that whole time, and our support team took the calls. The failure wasn't the slow index. It was that I planned around the happy path and never wrote down what we'd do if a step ran long. Since then I write a runbook for every risky change with a time box for each step and a rollback trigger, and I rehearse on production-sized data, even if that means sampling and scaling up. I've done three major-version upgrades since, and none took more than twenty minutes of degraded service.

answers.question: Describe your experience with cloud infrastructure, including AWS and Terraform.
answers.answer: I've built and run production services on AWS for about six years, and I've managed nearly all of that infrastructure in Terraform. On my current team I wrote the shared modules other teams use to stand up a service: networking, load balancing, a managed database, alerting and least-privilege access policies, with defaults chosen so a new service takes about forty lines of configuration. I care a lot about keeping state safe, so we split Terraform state per environment and per service, require plan output in every pull request, and run a nightly drift check that opens a ticket when someone changes something by hand in the console. I've also done the less glamorous work: splitting one giant state file into smaller ones without downtime, importing hand-built resources, and cutting our monthly AWS bill by about a third by right-sizing instances and adding lifecycle rules to old storage. When the provider documentation is unclear, I'm comfortable reading the provider source to find out what it actually does.

answers.question: Tell us about a time you had to make an important decision without all the information you wanted.
answers.answer: Last year a payment processor we depended on started returning intermittent errors on a busy weekend, and their status page said everything was fine. I was on call. I could see that about eight percent of charges were failing, but I couldn't tell whether the problem was on their side, in our network path, or in a recent change of ours. Waiting for certainty meant losing orders every minute, so I made a call with what I had. I rolled back our most recent deploy, since that was cheap and reversible, and when the errors continued I switched failed charges to a retry queue instead of showing customers an error. I posted each step and my reasoning in the incident channel as I went, so anyone could challenge it. The processor confirmed a regional outage about forty minutes later. The rollback turned out to be unnecessary, but it cost nothing, and the retry queue recovered nearly every order. What I took from it is to prefer the reversible action first and to write down why, so the decision can be judged on what I knew at the time.

answers.question: Why are you interested in Quillmate?
answers.answer: I write a lot at work, design docs, incident reviews, long pull request descriptions, and the slow part is never the typing. It's getting feedback from the right people before the doc goes stale. Quillmate is the first tool I've used that treats that as the real problem. I've used Quillmate Drafts for my own docs since the beta, and the review threads that stay attached to a paragraph even after it's rewritten changed how my team runs reviews: we stopped scheduling meetings just to walk through a doc. I want to work on a product where the people building it are also heavy users, because that's where small details get noticed and fixed. I also like that Quillmate is still small enough that a product engineer owns a feature from the database schema to the empty state. I've done that kind of end-to-end work before and it's when I do my best work. Tools for working together on writing are hard to get right, and I'd like to help get this one right.

answers.question: We believe exceptional performance in one area is a good indication of performance in other areas. Do you have any examples of exceptional performance you want to highlight?
answers.answer: Two examples. At work, I took over an on-call rotation that was paging about sixty times a week, and in three months I got it under ten by fixing the noisiest alerts at the source instead of tuning thresholds. Nobody asked me to. It was making good engineers want to quit, so I treated it as my main project for a quarter. Outside of work, I started running at thirty with no athletic background and finished a marathon in under three and a half hours two years later, using a training log I built myself to track mileage and recovery. Both came from the same habit: I pick one measurable thing, write the number down every week, and keep going after the first burst of enthusiasm wears off.

answers.question: Tell us about a time you received difficult feedback. How did you respond?
answers.answer: In my second year as a senior engineer, my manager told me that my code reviews were making newer engineers afraid to open pull requests. I was surprised, because I thought I was being thorough. When I reread my last twenty reviews, I saw what she meant: dozens of comments per review, no distinction between blocking issues and personal preferences, and almost never a note about what was good. I changed three things. I started labeling comments as blocking or optional, I moved style nits into a linter configuration so nobody had to argue about them, and I began each review with one sentence about what the change did well. A few months later, two of the newer engineers told me they'd started asking me for reviews on purpose. I still think about that feedback whenever I'm tempted to prove I'm right instead of helping someone ship.

answers.question: Is there anything else you'd like us to know?
answers.answer: One more thing worth mentioning: I've been a paying Quillmate user for two years, and I filed a few of the bug reports that ended up in your public changelog, including the one about comment threads disappearing after a paste. I also built a small command-line tool that exports Quillmate Drafts documents to plain text for our internal wiki, and I'd be glad to walk through it in an interview. I'm available to start after a four-week notice period.
